## The idea

A printed melody presents several dimensions at once. Reading pitch before meter
can produce correct note names in bars that have the wrong length. Choosing a
synth before encoding the score adds another variable while the transcription is
still unstable.

Use a fixed pass order: time signature, key signature, rhythm, pitches, ties,
then articulation. Each pass enriches the same event data. The order front-loads
structural checks. By the time sound enters, every bar should already total the
promised duration and every written accidental should have a recorded effect.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 92
use_synth :piano

# Four bars in 4/4, already resolved from a one-sharp key signature.
bars = [
  [[:g4, 1], [:a4, 1], [:b4, 1], [:d5, 1]],
  [[:c5, 0.5], [:b4, 0.5], [:a4, 1], [:g4, 2]],
  [[:d5, 1], [:c5, 1], [:b4, 0.5], [:a4, 0.5], [:fs4, 1]],
  [[:g4, 1], [:a4, 1], [:g4, 2]]
]

bars.each_with_index do |bar, index|
  total = bar.sum { |pitch, duration| duration }
  raise "bar #{index + 1} totals #{total}" unless total == 4
end

score = []
cursor = 0
bars.each do |bar|
  bar.each do |pitch, duration|
    score << {note: pitch, start: cursor, duration: duration}
    cursor += duration
  end
end

define :play_events do |events|
  cursor = 0
  events.each do |event|
    sleep event[:start] - cursor
    play event[:note], sustain: event[:duration] * 0.82,
      release: 0.08
    sleep event[:duration]
    cursor = event[:start] + event[:duration]
  end
end

puts "#{score.length} events, #{cursor} beats"
play_events score
```

The bar check runs before playback. Bar two ends with one two-beat G event, so a
tied pair from the source would produce one attack rather than two repeated Gs.
F-sharp in bar three records the key signature's default after resolution. The
renderer receives complete event data and adds no pitch decisions.

## Change one thing

1. Change bar three's last duration from `1` to `0.5`. The assertion stops the
   program before a malformed bar can be mistaken for a performance problem.
2. Split bar two's final G into two one-beat events. The total still passes, but
   you hear a second attack. This separates metric validation from tie handling.
3. Change synth and release only after restoring the valid data. Sound design
   alters interpretation while the decoded score remains inspectable.

## Why it works

The time signature gives an invariant: every 4/4 bar totals four quarter-note
beats. Rhythm can therefore be entered and checked before pitch. Key resolution
then converts spelling plus defaults into playable notes. Ties merge durations
across adjacent written values, and articulation becomes renderer metadata.

The bars are a source-facing representation. They preserve measure boundaries
for comparison with the page. The flattened score is renderer-facing and uses
absolute starts. Both views derive from the same arrays, avoiding a second manual
transcription.

Listening remains a separate validation pass. Compare one suspicious bar in a
loop against a lawful source recording when available. A bar total cannot detect
a wrong pitch, and Ruby syntax cannot detect a mistaken rhythm that still sums
to four. Structural assertions narrow the search; they do not certify fidelity.

Provenance is part of the data path. Keep the edition, page, system, and measure
number beside the transcription even when those fields never reach Sonic Pi.
When a note sounds doubtful, that pointer is cheaper than searching the score
again. It also separates a faithful encoding from an editorial change you make
because another voicing or articulation sounds preferable.

Part 9 begins by turning that pointer into a complete source record. Finish this
lesson with page and measure coordinates in place; Lesson 42 adds the edition,
rights statement, retrieval date, and redistribution decision before the
transcription grows beyond four bars.

## Take it further

Choose four printed bars from a public-domain score whose edition you can record.
Enter meter and rhythm first, and make every bar-total assertion pass. Add pitch
spelling, key-signature resolution, ties, and articulation in separate commits
or saved versions. Preserve source measure numbers in comments. Render the final
events without using a MIDI file, then list every point that still requires
manual comparison with the page or recording.
